idiom_name: final monitor class over a read-only policy table, handing out unforgeable capability handles
implementation_notes: The standard gives access specifiers - private members are reachable only from members and friends, checked at compile time - and deterministic destruction, which is enough to write the monitor as a final class in its own translation unit: private policy storage, a [[nodiscard]] decision function, no allocation and one member per mediated operation. What the language cannot give is tamper resistance: const_cast, reinterpret_cast, pointer arithmetic, a friend declaration added later, or simply linking a different object file all defeat the class, so in-process the monitor is a compile-time discipline whose real isolation comes from a process or kernel boundary. The capability half is where C++ is strong: hand out move-only handles whose constructors are private and whose only friend is the monitor, so possessing a handle is evidence that the monitor granted the access, and revocation means invalidating the handle rather than re-checking the caller.
pitfalls: Access specifiers are compile-time only: const_cast, reinterpret_cast, pointer arithmetic and memcpy reach private state at runtime, and adding a friend is a one-line change to the trust boundary.
Handing out a reference or pointer after a granted decision makes the check irrelevant - return capability handles, re-checking views or owned copies, never &resource.
virtual functions, std::function or std::any in the decision path place an object the caller can replace inside the monitor; keep the policy table immutable and the monitor's interface non-virtual.

Static initialisation order: a monitor that reads policy during another translation unit's static initialisation can decide against an empty table - construct on first use or pass the table in explicitly.
